game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you take the role of an investigator working for the government to investigate a series of terror attacks.

Throughout the game you are presented with lots of pieces of information which you have to upload to a person's "file" to establish a character background to see if they're involved in the terror attacks. I found this gameplay mechanic to be thrilling. You tap phones, computers, emails - pretty much everything! At points you are presented with conflicting information between the suspects. This is were the story can change. In a sort of telltale like manner, your choices affect the outcome of the game and your consequences are final. 

I really enjoyed this game and found myself enagaged with each episode. I do wish it was longer, or maybe had some DLC cases added.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ohh this is really, really well-done. To a large extent, this is what I've always wanted from a mystery game: being able to/having to think and reason for yourself, draw conclusions, then have them reflect in the game - rather than being taken through a sequence of 'revelations' by the game plot. Partially reminds me of old-school RPGs that didn't write down all the relevant information in the quest log for you and/or spell out the revelations and point you in the right direction - you had to put two and two together yourself. I actually took notes playing this game!

Things that made it a good mystery-like experience: Having to make judgement calls based on incomplete information. Occasional moments of adrenaline rush as you make genuinely (as far as I can tell as a player, anyway) time-sensitive calls. Real consequences that you can retroactively attribute to your actions (and adjust your strategy).

Story and gameplay integrate together very neatly. The Datachunk mechanic feels a bit hokey at first, until you realize that the system really does require your human judgement, and research beyond the highlighted datachunks, to work well.

Technically, this game is probably very easy to "complete", but I don't know if I would call any completion "beating" it.  I really felt clever when I figured out (part of) the mystery myself, and that actually affected the outcome.

Could probably write a whole paper on this game and questions like "what is winning/losing in a game?" "what is or is not gameplay?" "who is a villain and who is a hero?"  if one were inclined to write papers about new-media-like subjects.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

review_text_raw: Orwell is OKAY. Not great, but I enjoyed the experience for what it was; a visual novel. To be frank, the story basically plays itself out. You're just a passenger in this ride. The actual simulation of being an "investigator" is not fulfilled here whatsoever. Everything you can take note of is already highlighted for you. This is the gaming equivalent of sticking wooden blocks in their appropriate holes. It's a shame a political story as convoluted and detailed as Orwell's is matched with mindless "gameplay". I enjoyed the unique approach to storytelling and seeing the plot unravel with many twists and turns was engrossing. However, having your advisor constantly chime in after every single datachunk is submitted is annoying and unnecessary. There's no in-depth deduction system like the Sherlock Holmes games. Everything is filled in and connected for you. I find the topics of surveillance, civil unrest, immigration, etc. very fascinating, but to have the game straight up tell you what the right and wrong choices are takes away from the experience imo. I don't need the game to wag its finger at me for deciding that the terrorists belong in prison. The lack of nuance in how your very few choices are reflected in the end feels patronizing. In reality, with or without Orwell, there would be massive consequences. It's a very complex discussion, but the game ends before any discussion can really be had rushing through the final episode with a sloppy "I think we should do this, BUT IT'S UP TO YOU [insert player name here]!" choice at the end that just feels unearned. The concept and strong premise drew me in and the mystery kept me to the end. If you value deep forensics gameplay, look elsewhere. If you want a fairly compelling political thriller, this is not bad for the price. (6/10)

review_text_raw:
Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.

Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.

You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?

Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.

But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.

The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.

The game’s gameplay also shows how a system like that can lead to paranoia, as you see people engage in a lot of extremist rhetoric and it is easy to jump to conclusions and morally convict someone in your mind who didn’t do anything worse than complain, as well as how easy it is to prejudge someone in the opposite direction as well, making you think more positively of them than they truly deserve. And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.

How humane the system is – and who is in the right and wrong – is a complicated question that the game ultimately doesn’t answer for itself, but which the player answers via their actions throughout the game. Like “The Lady or the Tiger”, the way the player responds to the story really reflects as much on the player’s own evaluation of humanity, and how they weigh the risks and benefits of a system like that. Rather than being preachy about how evil the system is, the game also shows why people might like a system like that and want it to be implemented. It is perhaps the most even-handed presentation of the subject matter I’ve seen, and it achieves this by putting the player in the seat of someone who might be a part of such a system and showing just how ambiguous the system can be and how much power they wield, both how dangerous it can be if misused but how beneficial it can be if used appropriately.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell, the devil's in the details.

On my first playthrough, I thought that this was just a visual novel. I thought that conflicting datachunks were no big deal; I mean, I can just upload one of them and both will be sent to Orwell. Right?

Well, I was wrong, and that resulted in some very real consequences.

See, most of the game involves reading articles and personal information about people. Orwell cherry-picks information it wants and you upload it. Some information is clearly false or misinterpreted by the machine, so you can choose not to upload those chunks.

But once you've been lured into a false sense of security, a conflicting datachunk pops up. You have to decide, from the options provided, which is the real story. That, I've learned, requires you to go back and cover everything you've read with a fine-toothed comb.

That's where the game gets tough. After three episodes, I have made one, and maybe two, clear-cut mistakes with disastrous consequences. I'm not sure what I missed, but that's the fun of the game. Be meticulous. Pay attention to every tiny detail. Think very carefully before you choose which story to endorse, because Orwell will take it as fact.

review_text_raw:
One thing you won't read in most reviews is that Orwell plays with just a mouse. No keyboard required, except for creating a named profile at the very beginning (literally, just entering your character's name). 

So, Orwell, thanks for helping me pass the time after shoulder surgery!

Moving on to proper review:
I liked Orwell. It's a little bit 'Papers, Please', a little bit 'Her Story'. 

I'll speak vaguely so as to not spoil the game. Orwell starts a little slow and maybe feels too guided in the beginning. But by the end of the game, you're doing your own research and making decisions and interpretations that have consequences. It gets pretty intense towards the end, when you have limited time to get to the bottom of things. 

Looking through the community posts, it's clear that there are many branching paths and outcomes. (Seriously: Don't look at community posts before you've played the game.)

Research -> Decisions -> Consequences. So be careful with your research!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It’s timely that Orwell, the first game from Australian start-up Osmotic Studios delves into the muddy waters of government surveillance of its citizens, with the increasing nature of real world democracies doing the very same as they grapple with a world that is always connected and communicating.

Orwell opens with a deadly bombing in a public square that the player is tasked to investigate. This is achieved via a secret program codenamed Orwell, which allows an anonymous user, with the oversight of a supervisor, to snoop through social media posts, personal computers, bank statements and private correspondence of the suspects and associates.

My initial surveillance began with a singular suspect who had been caught by CCTV in the surrounding area and who had previously been arrested for attacking a police officer. My supervisor seemed to believe in this system, that malice lurked in unseen corners and that everyone was a potential threat.

From this one suspect a deeper conspiracy of activists emerged, and concerns of the erosion of liberties that were taken for granted by the citizens both fortified and weakened the idea of Orwell.

Continuing to spy on the fellow member’s activist group Thought reveals snippets of conversation that follow a story of mistrust of government and the over-reach of surveillance. Your actions, and inaction can and do have major consequences for those that you survey – and decisions on what you choose to upload to Orwell through a simple drag and drop interface can have fatal consequences and lock you to certain storylines.

Sifting through the large amount of data that the unknowing citizens freely make available reveals a story of love, betrayal, anger and sacrifice. I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time.

Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions.

The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. 

The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time.

8.2/10.

review_text_raw:
I wish I could give this a rating... Like "B+" or "70%".     

I came here having tried Orwell a few years ago and didn't take to it... Then I played "Return of the Obra Dinn" and was so entranced by it I searched for "Game like..." and this came up, so I went back and started over.

I'll just say that this game is NOTHING like "Return of the Obra Dinn".    It feels like the "Walking Simulator" of detective games. You don't 'detect' so to speak, more than you just walk through scads and scads of documents and photographs, and picking out important pieces that are pre-highlighted for you.  Occasionally you get to make a moral / ambiguous choice between two things with far too little / ambiguous information.   This is kind of the point of the game... To show how easily we can be led down a path of conclusion based on scant evidence... Is the player 'aware' enough of the situation to select the correct interpretation.  Sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's not.

Where Orwell falls down is that the consequence of what you pull out of the documentation isn't always clear.   You can be pulling out loads of stuff, with the occasional snide / snippy remark from your 'advisor', with no noticeable progress in the game.  Then all of a sudden, you pick something and *BOOM*  the whole world spins on its axis, and you suddenly get more context, albeit too late.

Now, as I said, the 'late information binding' thang is the whole Orwell shtick, but it's really s****g annoying when you're playing.  It's only in the end game, that the whole POINT of the game becomes clear and you realise that the annoyance you're feeling has a purpose.

Then the game offers you a moral choice...   Carry on, or rebel.  For me, the decision was pretty clear cut, but it didn't look like it had much effect, tbh.     And that's the other big issue, is that you're never sure if you chose correctly, wrongly, or your choice made no major difference.  Some might say this adds 'replayability', but to be honest, I don't think I can be bothered clicking through dozens of semi-meaningless PDFs for another 10 hours to choose different outcomes to test the theory....


I kinda enjoyed playing Orwell... But there were times when I just wanted the story to advance, but it simply refused because I had to make a choice.   And by this point, there was so little context, and so much cruft to wade through, I gave up and just picked one option to make the game carry on.   Perhaps that was the point as well.. I dunno. It's midnight and my brain hurts from reading all this text on the screen.

It's under a tenner on Steam right now. I can't remember how I got Orwell, but if I paid over £10, I don't think I got a good price/enjoyment ratio.    It's a relatively solid game, and has a fair point to make on the way the surveillance state is going, and had great music, good visuals and an interesting setting.  Get it if you like making your own deductions and choices.

You don't 'detect' so to speak, more than you just walk through scads and scads of documents and photographs, and picking out important pieces that are pre-highlighted for you. Occasionally you get to make a moral / ambiguous choice between two things with far too little / ambiguous information. This is kind of the point of the game... To show how easily we can be led down a path of conclusion based on scant evidence... Is the player 'aware' enough of the situation to select the correct interpretation. Sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's not. Where Orwell falls down is that the consequence of what you pull out of the documentation isn't always clear. You can be pulling out loads of stuff, with the occasional snide / snippy remark from your 'advisor', with no noticeable progress in the game. Then all of a sudden, you pick something and *BOOM* the whole world spins on its axis, and you suddenly get more context, albeit too late. Now, as I said, the 'late information binding' thang is the whole Orwell shtick, but it's really s****g annoying when you're playing. It's only in the end game, that the whole POINT of the game becomes clear and you realise that the annoyance you're feeling has a purpose. Then the game offers you a moral choice... Carry on, or rebel. For me, the decision was pretty clear cut, but it didn't look like it had much effect, tbh. And that's the other big issue, is that you're never sure if you chose correctly, wrongly, or your choice made no major difference. Some might say this adds 'replayability', but to be honest, I don't think I can be bothered clicking through dozens of semi-meaningless PDFs for another 10 hours to choose different outcomes to test the theory.... I kinda enjoyed playing Orwell... But there were times when I just wanted the story to advance, but it simply refused because I had to make a choice. And by this point, there was so little context, and so much cruft to wade through, I gave up and just picked one option to make the game carry on. Perhaps that was the point as well.. I dunno. It's midnight and my brain hurts from reading all this text on the screen. It's under a tenner on Steam right now. I can't remember how I got Orwell, but if I paid over £10, I don't think I got a good price/enjoyment ratio. It's a relatively solid game, and has a fair point to make on the way the surveillance state is going, and had great music, good visuals and an interesting setting. Get it if you like making your own deductions and choices.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A lightweight and interesting software title. "Orwell" is more of an interactive visual novel than a game, but tells a story well enough and the 2-4 hour playtime does not overstay too long. The plot is clear from the description and the marketing on Steam's storefront is accurate for what is offered - a tale of dystopia and hyper-surveillance where Your Choices Matter.

Much like "Papers, Please", there is a certain heroic conceit in an everyman investigator charting the path of the Nation, but the player will face real and weighty decisions with far-reaching consequences. By the mid-game, regular questions of guilt based on partial or contradictory evidence emerge and it will be up to you to decide what goes into the report and what does not. It can feel a little incomplete to mete out justice based on little more than social media posts and clipped messages from dubious surveillance, but I'll give a pass to the limited scope of the title because it is presented well and succeeds at reinforcing the message that privacy is complicated and imperfect.

The story also works well enough and there's some refreshing twists and dilemmas that keeps the plot intriguing so long as the player keeps up the tempo. I still feel like the later release of "Hypnospace Outlaw" is a better title in this game genre, but the commentary from "Orwell" about both security and authority are better storytelling than "Hypnospace" and does not disappoint. If you are like me then you'll only play it once and not again, but it's worth the $3 (USD) on sale to experience it and, if you're a fan of "1984", then this little simulation will fit you like a glove.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What an incredible game. I sat down hoping to start and finish a game in one sitting, and I did just that, just over 6 and a half hours later.

The game has you scouring websites and messages to begin with, later involving phone calls and electronic devices too. This action tickles a very specific investigative soft spot, allowing you to accept or reject information as you see fit (with some plot-progression-required points aside). Unfortunately this comes with the caviat that your -intention- is not always understood when making these choices, but the game does the best it can to inform you how the data will be interprited, while staying in-universe.

Now I have to make this very clear: I thought this game was completely different, based on the trailer I watched. I thought I would be monitoring areas using CCTV and pulling up profiles on potential criminals with Watchdogs-style hackery. This couldn't be further from the truth - this is an interactive visual novel through-and-though, much like a previous game I've played, and would highly recommend, Analogue: A Hate Story.

While playing this game I felt genuine emotions, which does not happen often. I felt elation at preventing an attack--something I felt I had complete control over, not just interaction with--and guilt over a death--one I know I caused, but could have potentially stopped with information I realised I had overlooked too late. It's like a more relaxed version of Telltale's The Walking Dead games, where your choices have sincere impact on the world. But don't think it's all just casual browsing either, as there are timed occurances that you need to be quick on your mouse to prevent, should you choose to. Sometimes you have to make uninformed choices, which you will simply have to live with the consequences of, while giving you hindsight for future playthroughs.

All in all, it was a fascinating story and premise that kept my attention for its duration, with the clear possibility of replayability, should you want to see all possible outcomes (and right your wrongs). You couldn't ask for more than that.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
As many others have mentioned, an interesting concept. Don't purchase this game looking for a good gameplay experience. This is certainly a visual novel with a little more interaction than usual, closing in on Point & Click Adventure territory.

It certainly has its own contemporary agenda, which they do a fairly good job at conveying. Its execution isn't always the best, some moments fall flat but are remedied by the pacing and -for me, personally- the desire to see what is going to happen next. While short, it offers enough of interest to be worth a purchase (perhaps at a 40-50% discount, depending on your tastes). 

The 'choices' you will encounter in this game usually boil down to 'jump to conclusion' and 'don't jump to conclusion', which can admittedly work out well in some cases. However, there are times where you will encounter unforseen consequences. These can definitely have an impact on how the game progresses, in increments. For the most part you are playing through a story on rails, with only a few forks in the road that eventually lead to the same place, anyways. The biggest choice you will get takes place at the end of the game, where you will most likely arrive after about 4 hours. 

I would say the game is worth playing for its subject matter alone, it stands on its own as an experience. Some food for thought is to be found, as well.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 312:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a tense, thought-provoking surveillance thriller that does more with a few browser tabs and text files than most games do with entire cities. It casts you as a government contractor sifting through personal data to uncover a growing threat—and forces you to wrestle with how much “truth” you really need to keep people safe. It’s slick, unsettling, and surprisingly emotional.

[b]🪬 Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Brilliant UI that doubles as storytelling. The whole game takes place inside a simulated desktop, with tabs for social media, chat logs, police records, and more. But it’s not just aesthetic! It feels like doing a job. Every click, every search result, every drag-and-drop data point creates tension. The interface is intuitive, immersive, and sinister.

[*] Deep moral ambiguity in every decision. Do you report that someone once expressed violent thoughts in a song lyric? Do you include their real name in a classified file? What about the context? The game forces you to make hard calls on limited info, and the consequences are immediate. 

[*] Tightly written and emotionally resonant. Despite being mostly text, the characters come alive through their messages, posts, and private calls. You start to see their contradictions, their fears, their humor. It’s intimate in a way that hits hard when you're the one deciding what gets flagged—and what gets buried.

[*] Great balance of investigation and puzzle-solving. The game isn’t about cracking codes or hacking firewalls: it’s about connecting dots. Who knows who? What’s fact, what’s hearsay, and what might get someone arrested? You feel clever when you catch a subtle connection between a dating profile and a news article. It’s simple but deeply satisfying.

[*] Fantastic pacing and structure. The game unfolds over five episodes, each building tension and complexity. Just when you think you know what’s going on, it flips your assumptions. It’s rare to find a game this compact that still manages to feel complete and impactful.
[/list]

👁️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Limited replay value. While your choices do have consequences, the story arc mostly funnels toward the same endpoint with slight variations. It’s a brilliant one-time experience, but it may not have the branching depth to support multiple playthroughs.

[*] Some plot twists feel a bit on-the-nose. The writing is mostly subtle, but a few characters and twists lean heavily into dystopian clichés. It's forgivable, especially for a debut game, but occasionally the nuance slips.

[*] A bit short. For players used to longer visual novels or narrative-driven games, [i]Orwell[/i] might feel more like an extended episode than a full series. That said, it’s tightly packed and doesn’t waste your time.
[/list]

[/url] Also, please leave a like and visit [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Indie_Gems]IndieGems[/url] and our YouTube channel for more reviews like this one.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
'Orwell' is a fascinating first-person adventure game that explores the implications of online surveillance -- by having the player act as Big Brother! You play an investigator tasked with capturing perpetrators responsible for a lethal bombing. With the help of an investigative advisor, you collect Datachunks to build profiles of suspects.

However, profile building is not a rote task because you'll need to pore through online documents, phone and chat transcripts, resolve conflicting information, and be judicious and definitive about which Datachunk to add to the profiles. Given that, your decisions in building a suspect's profile will have both short-term and long-term consequences, affecting how the story unfolds. 

'Orwell' makes players reflect on, or perhaps even reconsider the value of and impact of surveillance on public safety. It's both entertaining and thought-provoking, and I was compelled to replay it twice more so that I can see how different decisions will yield different outcomes. With such high value in entertainment, intellectual stimulation and replayability for its price, 'Orwell' gets my enthusiastic recommendation.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

It has several different endings, which are well-implemented, but the circumstances of the ending's gameplay were so muddled for me that I accidentally clicked my way into an ending I didn't want because I wasn't sure how to do what I wanted to do and I was loaded down with so much unprocessed information I had had to leave for later. The fact that the game jumps at the opportunity to end instead of letting you log out on your own terms when you've done what you want to do doesn't help. This critique probably makes more sense to those who have played it.

All in all, it's a brilliant little dystopia simulator with a lot of love and care poured into it, and a very pleasant and thought-provoking experience I highly recommend. Like any creation, it has its flaws, but it's well worth the price and you can tell how much work went into it.

review_text_raw:
Well-written game where your choices matter. Actions lead to consequences. Raises awareness about government surveillance over citizens and their privacy concerns.

The actual game design could use a lot more improvements, though. Why make the player wait for the information to upload? Why delay the player to sit through 10 minutes of conversation cutscenes? It's clear the game developer encourages replayability, but it's absolute cancer to sit through the exact same cutscenes just to change the ending a little bit? Pretty crappy thing to do for anybody playing the game more than once, (or for somebody playing your game for the third time just to get the Achievement Endings).
